142.t: Why he did not defect in 1979 and what changed in 1980
142.s: With a wife and young son held as hostages in effect, he stayed; the 1980 Peruvian Embassy crisis made him decide to leave on the next trip.
142.q: We keep traveling. We keep traveling, where did we go? Ah, we went to Mexico, we did Canada. A couple of times we did Canada. We play Montreal and Toronto and a couple of places there. And shortly after that we flew to Spain and I defected in Spain and came here six months later.

142.t: Deciding to defect on the May 1980 European tour
142.s: Broken instruments and the Mariel and embassy repression pushed him to leave on the tour; he told his wife he would try to bring her later.
142.q: For a tour; it was a tour in Europe. It was a tour of the southern countries and Spain, but then I decided that I was going to defect in the first port.

142.t: Walking out of the Madrid airport
142.s: At Madrid he claimed to forget his saxophone, took the street door instead of the plane, and a taxi to a friend's daughter whom he identified with a jewel.
142.q: The first port of entrance in Europe was Madrid, and there we have to wait for eight hours to take the plane to Sweden—I still have the ticket. I never board the plane.

142.t: The defection retold: the saxophone, Chucho and the police
142.s: He retells leaving the gate area, Chucho unaware, the wrong door, the jewel, and getting a temporary Spanish visa through the friend's daughter.
142.q: Well, ah, we took the Cubana aviation, flight from Havana to Madrid, was on a tour going to, I believe was Sweden. 30 years have passed, but I believe was Sweden we were going, and then we wait for six to eight hours in the airport. So, when they call the flight, I was extremely nervous, you know,…

142.t: How Cuban officials and bandmates reacted to his disappearance
142.s: Chaos broke out on the plane; Carlos Emilio later said officials were told he stayed to teach, and Enrique Pla said everyone knew he would eventually leave.
142.q: I didn’t make the flight, Carlos Emilio, he was our lead guitarist, later on when I saw him a year or two later, he told me that there was complete chaos in the plane; Chucho want to come back to Cuba, somebody told me that Chucho start crying, “How did this happen to me. We have to go back.” And…

142.t: His mother arrives and the US consul interviews him
142.s: His mother came within days and the American consul, wary of his Angola and Soviet travel, finally authorized the green card with a six-month wait.
142.q: So, we went to rent a place to stay, what they call, un hostel; it’s like a bed and breakfast, the Spanish version of American bed and breakfast. And then we immediately went to the American Embassy and applied for, for—what do you call it—a green card, but the thing is that my passport was totally…

142.t: Cuban control of musicians and why Chucho stayed
142.s: Defections continued, such as Arturo Sandoval's; he says Chucho promised his mother not to leave and accepted conditions, which Paquito could not do.
142.q: Yes; first of all it is not easy to leave your country forever. That is not an easy decision to say, ‘I am leaving everything, my marriage, my children, my house, my everything.’ And you are not going to come back; that is very hard to do, and second, I understand that Chucho promise his mother,…

142.t: Phoning Cuba with vinegar and salt
142.s: He called his family by tricking Madrid payphones with vinegar and salt, a Cuban and Vietnamese trick.
142.q: Very seldom. I was communicating with my former wife by telephone, in those days we didn’t have any emails or anything. So, telephone, and uh, there was a very interesting,

142.t: Political control of music and the exit-visa wait
142.s: After the revolution jazz was treated as the enemy, the state controlled what, when and with whom you played, and leaving required waiting up to twenty years.
142.ch: Army, politics and jazz in Cuba
142.q: Oh, when the war, it decide everything for your life; it’s impossible to do nothing, you know. You do things against all odds. For example, Jazz music, you want to play, you play Jazz all your life, that is what you want to do. Jazz is imperative, it represents the enemy, so why can’t I do now,…

397.t: Escaping Cuba in the Mariel boatlift
397.s: Peruvian Embassy crisis led Castro to open the port; Berroa escaped at 26 and arrived in May 1980.
397.q: I didn’t qualify. I escaped. Meaning, there was so much confusion. That was an event that surprised Castro, it really did. And the events, the Mariel events were happening because for at the Peruvian Embassy in Havana. A group of people took a bus and they slammed the bus into the Peruvian Embassy.…

397.t: Father's break with Castro and wanting to leave Cuba
397.s: His father turned against the revolution; youths persecuted for Beatles music made him want to leave.
397.q: I always, Monk, since I started using my mind, I’m also I have to say that my dad, who was a huge Fidel Castro fan up to the point that my father fought on Bay of Pigs defending the Cuban regime. In 1965 he broke ties with the revolution because he started seeing that Castro’s promises — that…

397.t: Father's embrace of and break with Castro's revolution
397.s: Berroa says his father fought at the Bay of Pigs, then turned against Castro around 1965 because the promises proved lies.
397.q: Yes. Like millions of Cubans, they embraced the Cuban revolution, I mean coming from a poor family so rightfully so my father was in Castro’s eyes because all of the promises that Castro made to the poor Cuban people, talking about equality, inclusion, and so forth and so on. So anyway, yes he did.…

397.t: Olympic athletes analogy on defection from socialist and capitalist countries
397.s: He argues that people flee Cuba and the Soviet bloc, not the reverse, and urges listeners to read about Eastern Europe.
397.q: countries. It has always been the other way around. Athletes from the former Soviet Union or the former Eastern European countries asking for political asylum. So in places like the United States or Belgium or France and any capitalist country where the game has been celebrated. So I think that…

397.t: Leaving Cuba by boat: banned music and the dream of jazz
397.s: He wanted freedom; Cuba's government opposed the Beatles and American jazz, so he decided to leave to play jazz and see his heroes.
397.q: Well first of all I was looking for freedom. In my case in particular my life in Cuba was unbearable. I never liked the system, just because the reason that I was not, I disagreed with the system that was against four guys from Liverpool with long hair and tight pants, three guitars and a drum. I…

362.t: Playing the bass at the American Embassy to get the green card
362.s: He borrowed a bass, got it past embassy security, and played Saints and You Are My Sunshine with an officer on guitar, winning his green card.
362.q: And I asked so many people, and so many American people were kind of laughing. They know what happens even inside the embassy, the American Embassy people were kind of laughing. And some guy just came out and he didn’t even see me but he just “don’t give up, don’t give up. Anyway, you can do it…

362.t: Overstaying a tourist visa and winning the green card lottery
362.s: He came on a three-month visa, overstayed nine years, then won a green card lottery but was told at the embassy to prove he was a musician.
362.q: Yeah. I thought I don’t have money, and I don’t have much time to earn money, because I wanted to really study jazz music. So I will just overstay. And I couldn’t get out, because therefore I couldn’t get out from the United States because I am overstaying. Nine years I did overstay. I just came as…

398.t: Escape attempts and what happens to men caught in Mississippi
398.s: Few escapes succeed; men caught are sent back, or serve time in Mississippi first for a new crime.
398.q: Well, it had been some tried it, didn't make it. It had been some tried it and made it. Some tried it on the way, some got caught on the way, and some went across to the other side and still got caught.

399.t: Leaving Cuba in 1967 after Castro's military decree
399.s: Hearing Castro's speech in his father's car, Conte was sent out alone at 14; the cover story was a wish to become a priest, and his parents did not see him for seven years.
399.ch: Leaving Cuba and arriving in Los Angeles
399.q: Well it didn’t start at the dinner table, it started while I was in a car with my dad. And my dad would make house – he was a doctor so he was making house visits. And sometimes I would go with him, for whatever reason. And Castro was over there when Mr. Castro or whoever is in power now speaks…
